[Module 11](/learn/modules/11-cloud/#implementation) shows a `FailoverController` that "only
triggers once every health check inside the RTO window has failed", and says that ties the failover
trigger to the RTO it is meant to honour. This lab runs that controller — and the obvious
alternative — over simulated regions, and measures what it actually does to recovery time.

Source: [`labs/region-failover-budget`](https://github.com/vins13pattar/principal-ai-engineer-handbook/tree/main/labs/region-failover-budget)

<Aside type="caution" title="production-shaped: there is no cloud here">
  Regions, probes, transient blips, and outages are a **seeded discrete-event simulation**, and the
  same seed prints byte-identical output. Blips arrive as a Poisson process and last an
  exponentially distributed time — that assumption drives every false-failover number, so it is
  printed with every result. The downstream stages of a failover (promotion, traffic shift,
  capacity, loading weights) are **inputs, not measurements**: round defaults for you to replace
  with your platform's. Detection is the one stage the lab measures.
</Aside>

## The finding

A window trigger cannot fire until the whole window has been unhealthy, so **detection alone takes
the window**. Everything else a failover does happens after that — and for AI serving, everything
else includes loading the model onto the standby's GPUs. At the defaults (a 15-minute RTO, 60 s
promotion, 120 s traffic shift, 140 GB of weights at 1 GB/s):

| Trigger                       | Detection | Hot standby | Warm standby | Cold standby |
| ----------------------------- | --------- | ----------- | ------------ | ------------ |
| Window = RTO (900 s), as Module 11 describes | 900 s | 1,080 s — **over** | 1,220 s — **over** | 1,820 s — **over** |
| Window = 300 s                | 300 s     | 480 s       | 620 s        | 1,220 s — over |
| 12 consecutive failures       | 110 s     | 290 s       | 430 s        | 1,030 s — over |

Set the window to the RTO and recovery misses the RTO on **every** tier, including a hot standby
that has nothing to warm. The window has to be sized from what the RTO leaves _after_ the
downstream stages — 720 s for hot, 580 s for warm here — not from the RTO itself. And the cold row
is the other half of the lesson: with 140 GB to load and capacity to find, no trigger can meet a
15-minute RTO at all. That is a standby-tier decision, and no amount of trigger tuning recovers it.

## The other side: eager triggers fail over on blips

Shorten the window and false failovers arrive. Over 30 simulated days at the default blip rate (4
an hour, mean 20 s):

| Trigger              | False failovers / day | Detection |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | --------- |
| 1 failed probe       | 71.7                  | 0 s       |
| 3 consecutive        | 25.3                  | 20 s      |
| 6 consecutive        | 6.0                   | 50 s      |
| Window 60 s          | 3.3                   | 60 s      |
| 12 consecutive       | 0.2                   | 110 s     |
| Window 300 s         | 0.0                   | 300 s     |

Two things are worth reading out of this. First, **the shape of the rule matters less than its
patience**: a window of `W` seconds behaves like `W / interval + 1` consecutive failures, and the
two families interleave in one ordering by how long they wait. Second, **every number here moves
with the blip distribution**. Triple the mean blip length to 60 s and 12 consecutive failures goes
from 0.2 false failovers a day to 13.2. The shape — more patience, fewer false failovers, later
detection — holds under both settings, and that is what the tests assert. The magnitudes are yours
to measure on your own probe history.

## Silence is read as health

The module's controller returns `False` when its window holds no checks. An outage that takes the
prober down with the region produces exactly that: no checks. **The controller never fails over.**

In the sweep, it caught a dark region in 2 of 30 runs — both by luck, where the region happened to
go dark mid-blip, so the last checks it held were unhealthy and outlived the healthy ones. Counting
a probe that was due and never arrived as a failure (`silence_is_failure=True`) catches all 30,
under every trigger.

## A restarted controller fails over on its first bad probe

With no history, one unhealthy check is every check in the window, so a freshly started controller
fires on the first unhealthy probe it sees. A controller that restarts — a deploy, a crashed pod —
during a blip fails the region over immediately. `tests/test_triggers.py` pins it. The fix is a
minimum history before the trigger is armed, which is the same idea as the window itself.

## What is not here

- **RPO and replication lag**, Module 11's third failure mode. An honest simulation needs a model
  of how replication lag behaves under the load that precedes an outage, and any such model would
  bake in the conclusion it was meant to test.
- **IAM blast radius**, which the [Agent Identity Broker](/build/labs/agent-identity-broker/) lab
  already measures.

## Run it

```bash
cd labs/region-failover-budget
uv venv && uv pip install -e '.[dev]'
.venv/bin/python -m failover_budget                     # 30 seeds, RTO 900 s
.venv/bin/python -m failover_budget --rto 300 --blip-mean 60
```

The run takes about a second. Gates are `ruff`, `mypy --strict src tests`, and `pytest`; every test
asserts a shape, never a count.

## Principal-level discussion points

- **Where does your RTO actually go?** Write the budget out stage by stage before choosing a
  detection threshold. If the downstream stages already exceed the RTO, the conversation is about
  standby tier and model size, not health checks.
- **Who owns the false-failover rate?** A failover is itself an incident — it moves traffic, cold
  caches, and pages people. The trigger's patience is a policy choice with an owner, and it should
  be re-fit from real probe history, not set once from intuition.
- **What does your controller do when the signal disappears?** Absence of evidence is the most
  common shape of a regional outage's first minute. Decide, in code, whether silence is health.
